title: The Oyster Helpers Trying to Bring Back Chesapeake Bay
summary:
John Consoli leans over his pier on Maryland's Kent Island and hauls up a mesh bag, packed like a pillowcase, out of the Chesapeake Bay. Inside are oysters from this year. In just three months, he says, they have grown so much that he can hardly pull the net up.

Consoli loves these rock-like creatures because of the good they do. Each adult oyster filters up to 50 gallons of water a day. Cleaner water helps the bay and sea grass, which helps crabs and other organisms. Oyster shells, full of nooks and crannies, also give small fish and crabs places to live, eat and hide. Consoli even found a seahorse among them once.

Oyster reefs used to abound in the Chesapeake, but overharvesting reduced them by over 99% by 2011, according to one estimate. That hurt water quality and habitat. Farming has expanded in recent years and wild oysters have made a partial comeback, helped by better management and restoration, biologist Ryan Carnegie says. But fisheries oceanographer Elizabeth North says current populations are likely still a fraction of historic populations.

Consoli floats his oysters just below the surface to help them grow, and he recruits neighbours through what he calls his Peer to Pier Network. His wife, Kathy, says he may have reached 80 people. In August, he worked with a local restaurant to place a million baby oysters around its dock pilings.

Robots may help too. Engineer Miao Yu's team uses a raft-like robot called Oysterbot, with sonar below, and a smaller underwater robot to map the seabed. With AI, they hope to turn those images into maps showing farmers where oysters are, and when and where to plant and harvest.
why_it_matters: Cleaner bay water helps sea grass, crabs and other organisms that depend on the Chesapeake. The recovery work shows how local volunteers and new technology can help repair a damaged habitat.

background_read: Chesapeake Bay is a large bay where oysters once formed huge reefs along the bottom.
Oysters help the bay because each adult filters water as it feeds, and their shells give small fish and crabs places to live, eat and hide.
Overharvesting reduced the bay's oysters greatly, which hurt water quality and habitat.
Now farmers, volunteers and better management are helping oysters make a partial comeback, and new tools such as underwater robots may help people plant and harvest them wisely.
